title: The establishment of the Weimar Republic and its early problems

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 3, key topic 1. Read more: Payne, Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Germany, chapter 1 (pp. 2–23).

learn.intro: In November 1918 the Kaiser abdicated and Germany became a democracy. Within five years the new Weimar Republic faced a hated peace treaty, uprisings from left and right, a French invasion of the Ruhr and hyperinflation.

sections.title: 1. The Kaiser's abdication and the German Revolution, 1918–19

blocks.p: By autumn 1918 Germany was losing the war and its people were starving because of the British naval blockade. In late October sailors at Kiel mutinied rather than sail on a final mission. Workers' and soldiers' councils took control in many cities.

On 9 November 1918 Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated and fled to the Netherlands. Friedrich Ebert, leader of the Social Democrats (SPD), became head of government and a republic was declared. Two days later, on 11 November, the new government signed the armistice ending the fighting.
Elections in January 1919 chose a National Assembly. Because Berlin was dangerous, it met in the quiet town of Weimar — giving the Republic its name.

evidence: January 1919: National Assembly elected; meets at Weimar.

sections.title: 2. The Weimar Constitution: strengths and weaknesses

ul: Strength: very democratic — men and women over 20 could vote; the Reichstag was elected every four years.
Strength: a Bill of Rights guaranteed freedoms such as free speech and religion.
Weakness: proportional representation meant many small parties, so governments were coalitions that often collapsed.
Weakness: Article 48 let the President rule by decree in an emergency — later used to bypass the Reichstag.
Weakness: judges, army officers and civil servants from the Kaiser's time stayed in their jobs, and many disliked the Republic.

evidence: Votes for men and women over 20.
President elected every 7 years; Article 48 emergency powers.

sections.title: 3. Reactions to the Treaty of Versailles

blocks.p: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919. Germany lost about 13 per cent of its land, including Alsace-Lorraine and land given to Poland, and all its colonies. Its army was limited to 100,000 men, with no tanks, air force or submarines, and the Rhineland was demilitarised. Under the 'war guilt' clause (Article 231) Germany accepted blame for the war, and in 1921 reparations were set at £6,600 million.

Germans were furious. They called it a Diktat — a dictated peace — because they had not been allowed to negotiate. The politicians who signed it were called the 'November criminals', and many believed the 'stab in the back' myth that the army had been betrayed by politicians. The Republic was linked with humiliation from the start.

sections.title: 4. Challenges from the Left and Right

blocks.p: Left: in January 1919 the communist Spartacists, led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, tried to seize power in Berlin. Ebert used the army and the Freikorps — ex-soldiers who hated communism — to crush the rising. Luxemburg and Liebknecht were murdered.

Right: in March 1920 Wolfgang Kapp led Freikorps units into Berlin in the Kapp Putsch. The army refused to stop them and the government fled. Workers in Berlin called a general strike; with the city at a standstill, Kapp gave up within days.
Right-wing extremists also murdered politicians, including Matthias Erzberger (1921) and Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau (1922). Judges often gave right-wing offenders light sentences.

evidence: March 1920: Kapp Putsch defeated by a general strike.

sections.title: 5. The Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation, 1923

blocks.p: When Germany failed to make a reparations payment, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, Germany's main industrial area, in January 1923, to take goods instead. The government told workers to use passive resistance — to go on strike — and kept paying them by printing more money.

Causes of hyperinflation: the government had already printed money to pay for the war; reparations drained gold and goods; the Ruhr occupation cut production while the government printed even more money. By November 1923 a loaf of bread cost about 200 billion marks.

Effects: savers, pensioners and people on fixed incomes were ruined; wages could not keep up with prices; some people bartered goods. But some gained: people who had borrowed money paid off debts cheaply, and some businessmen bought up property. Many middle-class Germans blamed the Republic.

evidence: January 1923: French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr.
November 1923: a loaf of bread cost about 200 billion marks.
